title: Ecological threshold

definition.text: The point at which a fairly small change in outside conditions sets off a rapid change in an ecosystem.

facts.text: Once a threshold is passed, the ecosystem may not be able to return to its earlier state through its own resilience.
Thresholds show that ecosystems respond non-linearly to pressures from human activity or natural processes.
Thresholds can be sharp points or zones in which the shift from one state to another is gradual.
Many crossed thresholds have proved hard or nearly impossible to undo, which is why they are called points of no return; extinction is a definitive example.
Thresholds often show hysteresis: the way back from the altered state can be very different from the path that led there.
Detecting a threshold is not always easy; one approach scans time series for a sudden jump.
Clear lakes turning turbid is a well documented example, and a database by the Resilience Alliance and Santa Fe Institute lists over one hundred cases.
Critical load, regime shift, critical transition and tipping point are closely related terms.

related: Tipping points in the climate system

definition.text: The largest population of a species that a particular environment can keep going over time, given its food, habitat, water and other resources.

facts.text: At carrying capacity, births equal deaths (plus immigration and emigration), so the population is in equilibrium.
Below carrying capacity a population can grow; above it, the population usually shrinks for lack of space, food or sunlight.
The factor that stops a population growing, such as food, water, nesting space or the waste the environment can absorb, is called a limiting factor.
Applied to an environment as a whole, carrying capacity means resources are not taken faster than they regrow and wastes stay within what nature can absorb.
The idea is used to find the maximum population an environment can support in ecology, agriculture and fisheries.
The term spread through biology in the 1870s, was developed in wildlife and livestock management in the early 1900s and became a staple of ecology by the 1950s.
Many authors doubt its usefulness for wild populations, since it can oversimplify how species interact.

definition.text: A population model in which growth slows as numbers approach the carrying capacity K and stops at K.

facts.text: Verhulst's equation is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), where N is population size, r the intrinsic rate of natural increase and K the carrying capacity.
When the population is small it grows exponentially; as it nears K, growth falls and reaches zero.
Solving the equation gives the S-shaped logistic growth curve N(t) = K/(1 + Ae^(−rt)).
The letter K comes from the German Kapazitätsgrenze, meaning capacity limit.
Pierre François Verhulst published the equations in 1838 without using the term carrying capacity.

definition.text: In farming, the number of livestock a piece of land can carry, used to set a sustainable stocking rate.

facts.text: Hadwen and Palmer (1923) defined carrying capacity as the density of stock that could graze for a set period without damaging the range.
In Australia paddock capacity is counted in Dry Sheep Equivalents; one DSE is a 50 kg Merino wether or dry ewe kept in stable condition.
Other countries use other units; the United Kingdom measures paddocks in livestock units.

title: Human carrying capacity

definition.text: The number of people the Earth or a region can support, which depends on how people live and the technology they use.

facts.text: The agricultural and industrial revolutions raised human carrying capacity, letting population grow from 5 to 10 million in 10,000 BCE to 1.5 billion in 1900.
Without the Haber-Bosch process for fixing nitrogen, modern agriculture could not support 8 billion people.
These successes have come at grave environmental cost, including climate change, ocean acidification and dead zones at river mouths.
Degrading the ecosystem services people depend on could lower Earth's human carrying capacity; some argue 8 billion may already be above it.
Measuring it is arbitrary: choices about what counts as food or water, and the fact that regions trade resources, change the answer.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005, involving more than 1,300 experts, warned that rapid ecosystem change threatens long-term human carrying capacity.
Crossing one planetary boundary does not prove carrying capacity is exceeded, but crossing several makes that harder to deny.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether today's human population already exceeds Earth's long-run carrying capacity and how far technology can raise it.

title: Planetary boundaries

definition.text: A framework that sets limits on how far human activity can push the Earth system before it may stop regulating itself.

facts.text: Crossing the limits could push the Earth system out of the stable Holocene period in which human society developed.

The nine boundaries are climate change, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone depletion, nitrogen and phosphorus flows, freshwater use, land system change, biosphere integrity, chemical pollution and atmospheric aerosol loading.
Its authors warned that transgressing boundaries risks crossing thresholds that trigger non-linear, abrupt change at continental to planetary scale.
The framework was developed in 2009 by scientists led by Johan Rockström of the Stockholm Resilience Centre and Will Steffen of the Australian National University.
In 2009 three boundaries were judged crossed; the 2015 update found four crossed.
Novel entities were judged the 5th transgressed boundary in 2022, freshwater change the 6th in 2023 and ocean acidification the 7th in 2025.
Agriculture and food contribute to the transgression of four of the nine boundaries, with surplus nitrogen and phosphorus flows most important.
UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon endorsed the concept in 2012, though it was later dropped from the Rio+20 text over poorer countries' worries about sidelining development.

related: Tipping points in the climate system

definition.text: The measurable quantities and limit values the framework uses to track how far humanity has shifted the Earth away from Holocene conditions.

facts.text: The 2009 study quantified seven of the nine boundaries; by 2025 eight were quantified.
The climate boundary is 350 ppm of atmospheric CO2, against a current 423 ppm and a pre-industrial 280 ppm.
The biosphere integrity boundary is under 10 extinctions per million species-years, while the current rate is over 100.
The land system boundary keeps 75% of forests intact; the global figure is 59%.
Industrial and intentional nitrogen fixation has a boundary of 62 Tg per year against a current 165 Tg per year.
Aerosol loading and stratospheric ozone depletion are the two boundaries listed as not exceeded.
For several processes no single threshold point can be located, because the Earth system is complex and evidence is still partial.

definition.text: The zone inside the planetary boundaries where Holocene-like conditions can be kept and risks to societies stay low.

facts.text: Each control variable has a range of values; the boundary is set at the lower end of that range.
Beyond the range lies a poorly predictable world, and persistent crossing pushes the world further into a danger zone.
The authors framed boundaries as a safe space for human development, an advance on simply minimising human impact.

definition.text: The ways that pushing one planetary boundary changes the safe level of others.

facts.text: The authors suggested a crossed boundary shrinks the safe operating space for other processes rather than enlarging it.
For example, breaching the freshwater boundary could make land arid and lower the land-use boundary.
Warming, acidity and UV together stress marine life far more than any single stressor alone.

definition.text: The healthy functioning of Earth's life-support systems, also called ecological integrity.

facts.text: Scholars say planetary integrity must be maintained for long-term sustainability.

title: Critiques of planetary boundaries

definition.text: The arguments over whether fixed global limits are a fair and useful guide for environmental policy.

facts.text: Development scholars argue forest-conservation targets reward rich countries that already cleared their forests while asking poorer ones to sacrifice.
William Schlesinger warns that managing to a threshold lets slow, diffuse degradation persist almost indefinitely.
Critics note the framework treats the Holocene as a safe zone even though it never involved industrial farming.
Supporters say it highlights the risk of abrupt, non-linear change and can help build agreements on threats such as climate change.

contested_note: Scholars dispute whether planetary boundaries are fair to the Global South and whether threshold-based management works.
